title: Reconciling growth mindset with cognitive science
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a skeptic who ended up on her school's team implementing growth mindset, tests which of its strategies survive contact with cognitive science. She keeps three: focusing on process as well as product, attributing outcomes to controllable causes, and setting high expectations while embracing struggle. For each she ties the strategy to evidence-based classroom practice, such as declarative and procedural knowledge, retrieval practice and self-quizzing, sequenced lessons, clear routines and Lemov's ratio technique. She is explicit that effort talk and constant praise will not make much difference on their own. Her conclusion is modest: use the sensible parts of growth mindset alongside cognitive science and let evidence guide what to keep or dismiss. It is a practitioner's reconciliation rather than a research review.
points: Process matters because correct answers rest on declarative and procedural knowledge, and exam boards award marks for steps shown.
Telling students that outcomes are controllable only helps if teachers also teach strategies such as retrieval practice and self-quizzing.
High expectations require well-sequenced lessons, routines, questioning and gradual removal of scaffolds so all students can access hard content.
Productive struggle can be checked by the right ratio, where all students are thinking hard and participating.
quotes: Slowly, I realised that while I still didn’t think only talking about effort and providing praise all the time was going to make much difference to my students, there were a few things that made sense and could also be linked to cognitive science.

By setting high expectations, we are sending our students the message that they can do the work. All our classes can do well if they can access the content. And to enable them to access the content, we need to have perfectly sequenced lessons, clear routines, lots of retrieval practice, quality questioning, and a gradual removal of scaffolding to help our students gain the confidence to do the tasks independently.

Embracing struggle can be achieved by having the right ratio (a TLAC technique, perfectly explained by Adam Boxer here) in our classrooms. If all our students are thinking and participating hard, then they are experiencing the right type of struggle, something we should actively encourage.

It has certainly challenged my own views on what is important and what we should dismiss. Ultimately, our goal is help our students achieve and as long as we use evidence as our guide, we will get there.
